title: Zoom in: how membership places a node's virtual nodes before publishing a ring
caption: Token count follows machine size, and the ring is checked for even shares before any app server sees it.

steps.text: Cache D joins with the same size as the others, so weight 1.
Hash D#0 … D#127 to 128 positions spread pseudo-randomly around the ring.
Merge them into the sorted token array. Each token takes a small slice from whichever arc it lands in.
Before publishing, compute every physical node's total arc length. With 128 random tokens a spread of about ±10% is normal; refuse only real outliers.
With 128 tokens per node the shares are close, so the new ring goes out to the app servers.

scenarios.name: Bigger machine
scenarios.summary: Weight is just more tokens: a node with twice the memory gets 256 tokens and about twice the keys.

steps.text: Cache C is replaced by a box with twice the RAM: weight 2.
256 tokens instead of 128, so its arcs add up to about twice the others'.
The check compares each node's share with its weight, not with a flat average.

scenarios.name: Node removed
scenarios.summary: Deleting tokens is the same process in reverse; each removed arc merges into the next one clockwise.

steps.text: Its 128 tokens are deleted from the array; nothing new is hashed.
Its arcs merge into 128 different neighbours, so the survivors each grow a little.

scenarios.name: Too few tokens
scenarios.summary: With a handful of tokens per node, arc lengths vary wildly; refuse to publish a ring that would overload one node.

steps.text: Someone configures 4 tokens per node to keep the ring tiny.
Four random points per node leave some arcs several times longer than others.
One node's share is well over 1.25× the average: it would take far more than its share of keys and traffic.
Hold the change and alert. Raise the token count; the ring stays small anyway (a few thousand entries).
